To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a dendritic amplifier, consisting of a potassium conductance at the soma and a calcium conductance in the distal apical trunk, linearizes and amplifies synaptic inputs, and (b) the amplifier's output is proportional to the input current, and thus the amplifier can be modeled with a simple linear transfer function.

1. the dendritic tree can act as an amplifier that can amplify synaptic input by a factor that depends on the position of the synapse in the apical dendrite, 2. the dendritic amplifier has the ability to linearize the synaptic current, 3. the amplifier can be used for the purpose of signal summation, and 4. the amplifier can amplify synaptic inputs to a level that allows them to drive the soma to spike.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the dendritic tree can be used to enhance and linearize the input to a pyramidal neuron.
the mechanisms that underlie the amplification of apical inputs to pyramidal cells.
a new mechanism that can be used to understand how neurons process information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the apical tufts of cortical pyramidal cells have evolved a mechanism that allows them to faithfully transmit synaptic input from distal synapses to their somatic output.
dendritic amplification of distal synaptic input is an essential mechanism for the proper function of cortical pyramidal neurons.
the amplifying mechanism is an important and necessary part of the dendritic tree.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dendritic spikes are not a special feature of pyramidal neurons, but rather a natural and necessary consequence of the amplification of synaptic inputs.
the apical trunk of a layer 5 pyrmidal neuron is a low-pass linear filter with a gain that is proportional to its input current.
dendrites are not only passive cables, but also contain a complex array of conductances that can be used to shape the electrical properties of the neuron.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a simple, linear amplifier in the apical dendrites of pyramidal cells can provide a mechanism for amplifying and linearizing distal inputs to the soma, which may be important for the computation and transmission of information in cortical circuits.
the same conductances that are thought to generate the complex dendritic spikes and plateaus are also involved in the linear amplification of synaptic inputs.

the same conductance mechanisms can be recruited for two distinct and seemingly contradictory functions: (1) amplifying and linearizing distal inputs, and (2) generating the complex spikes that are often used as a signature for dendritic computation.
